body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Early mobilisation in mechanically ventilated adults and ICU-acquired weakness: a randomised trial","authors":"Brennan-Adeyemi C, Solberg-Mwangi T, Iqbal-Fontaine R","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Critical Care Rehabilitation","doi":"10.5555/jccr.2019.0152","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 200 adults expected to be ventilated for more than 48 hours to early mobilisation led by physiotherapists from the first day of stability, or to usual care with mobilisation when clinicians judged it appropriate. ICU-acquired weakness at ICU discharge, defined as an MRC sum score below 48, occurred in 27 percent with early mobilisation and 41 percent with usual care. Functional independence at hospital discharge was 52 percent and 38 percent. Adverse events during mobilisation occurred in 1 percent of sessions, none serious. The trial was at two centres with experienced physiotherapy teams."},{"title":"Early mobilisation in critically ill adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of muscle strength and function","authors":"Takahashi-Oyelaran M, Delgado-Hurst P, Nkemelu-Strand A","year":2022,"venue":"Intensive Care Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/icer.2022.0209","providerType":"meta-analysis","abstract":"We included 16 randomised trials of early mobilisation in critically ill adults. Early mobilisation reduced ICU-acquired weakness (risk ratio 0.70, 95 percent CI 0.55 to 0.89) and improved function at discharge, with no difference in mortality. Trials varied widely in the timing and dose of mobilisation, and most compared an enhanced programme with little mobilisation rather than with partial adherence to a protocol. Adverse events were rare and none was fatal. Certainty was moderate for weakness and low for function, and no trial reported outcomes beyond hospital discharge."},{"title":"Barriers to mobilisation in intensive care: a multicentre point-prevalence study","authors":"Vasquez-Lindqvist J, Okafor-Barnes E","year":2021,"venue":"Critical Care Practice Reports","providerType":"cross-sectional study","abstract":"On two survey days, 38 intensive care units recorded whether each patient was mobilised and the main reason if not. Patients were mobilised on 36 percent of patient-days. Sedation was the most common barrier, recorded on 42 percent of days without mobilisation, followed by haemodynamic instability and staff availability. Units with a dedicated physiotherapist and a daily sedation interruption protocol mobilised more patients. Barrier recording depended on staff judgement and may have been inconsistent between units, and weekend days were not sampled."},{"title":"Illness severity and the association between immobility and ICU-acquired weakness: a cohort analysis","authors":"Haddad-Kowalski S, Ferreira-Nnamdi O, Lund-Achebe K","year":2018,"venue":"Critical Care Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/cce.2018.0073","providerType":"cohort study","abstract":"In 640 ventilated adults, we examined the association between days without mobilisation in the first week and ICU-acquired weakness at discharge. The crude odds ratio was 3.1 per three days without mobilisation, which fell to 1.4 (95 percent CI 0.9 to 2.2) after adjustment for illness severity score, days of deep sedation, sepsis and corticosteroid use. Sicker patients were both less often mobilised and more often weak. The authors conclude that observational estimates are strongly confounded by severity and recommend restriction to patients eligible for mobilisation on each day."},{"title":"The ICU Mobility Scale on day 3 as a marker of later ICU-acquired weakness: a diagnostic accuracy study","authors":"Olsen-Ubah R, Castellanos-Reid D","year":2024,"venue":"Critical Care Measurement","doi":"10.5555/ccm.2024.0038","providerType":"diagnostic accuracy study","abstract":"We assessed whether the ICU Mobility Scale on day 3 identified 312 ventilated adults who would have ICU-acquired weakness at discharge. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.71. At a threshold below 3, sensitivity was 68 percent and specificity 64 percent. Patients who were sedated on day 3 could not be scored and were excluded, which may have inflated accuracy. The authors suggest the scale is too inaccurate on its own to target interventions but may add to a risk score."},{"title":"Length of stay attributable to ICU-acquired weakness: a matched analysis","authors":"Grant-Sato M, Mahlaba-Pryce J","year":2020,"venue":"Intensive Care Health Services Research","doi":"10.5555/ichsr.2020.0117","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We matched 220 patients with ICU-acquired weakness to 220 without it on age, admission diagnosis, illness severity and days of ventilation. Weakness was associated with 4.2 additional ICU days and 9 additional hospital days. Costs were not reported directly, but the authors note that ICU days are the most expensive part of an admission. Matching could not remove differences in sedation practice, and patients who died in the ICU were excluded, so the attributable stay may be overestimated. The analysis did not examine mobilisation."},{"title":"Nurses' and physiotherapists' views of early mobilisation in intensive care: a focus group study","authors":"Whitaker-Oduya L, Benedetti-Kariuki S","year":2016,"venue":"Nursing in Critical Care Research","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We held focus groups with 26 nurses and physiotherapists in three intensive care units. Staff supported early mobilisation but feared dislodging lines and tubes, particularly at night and at weekends when fewer physiotherapists were present. Responsibility for deciding that a patient was ready to mobilise was often unclear. Staff described documentation of mobilisation as incomplete because it was recorded in several places. Participants suggested a single daily readiness decision recorded by the bedside nurse, with the physiotherapist confirming the plan at the morning round."}]}
